steps.say: A newborn baby has a heart dominated by the right ventricle, so the electrical tracing looks very different from an adult tracing. The QRS axis points far to the right, between plus 110 and plus 180 degrees, and lead V1 shows a tall R wave. Recognising this normal pattern stops you from wrongly diagnosing right ventricular hypertrophy in a healthy neonate.
steps.tx: Healthy neonates show **physiological right ventricular dominance** because the right ventricle did the bulk of fetal work against high pulmonary resistance. The frontal QRS axis lies between **+110 to +180 degrees**, right precordial leads show prominent R waves, and these rightward forces regress steadily as the left ventricle gains dominance over the first months of life.

steps.say: Parents often worry when a child tracing shows upside down T waves across the right chest leads. This juvenile T wave pattern is completely normal through the early school years. The T wave in V1 stays upright for only the first 48 to 72 hours of life, then it inverts and usually remains inverted until 6 to 8 years of age.
steps.tx: The **juvenile T wave pattern** is normal **T wave inversion in V1** and the neighbouring right precordial leads throughout early childhood. The T wave in lead V1 is upright for the first **48-72 hours** of life, then inverts and stays inverted until **6-8 years** of age, sometimes persisting into adolescence, so isolated T inversion in V1 needs no cardiac workup in this window.

vis.alt: Twelve lead electrocardiogram showing deep symmetric T wave inversion in the anterior chest leads with preserved R waves.
vis.caption: Anterior T wave inversion resembling the benign juvenile pattern of childhood. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.say: The same upright T wave that is normal on day one becomes a warning sign a week later. When the T wave in V1 stays upright between 7 days and 6 years of age, after the early newborn period has passed, it points reliably toward right ventricular hypertrophy. This single observation is one of the most sensitive bedside clues to pressure or volume loading of the right ventricle.
steps.tx: An **abnormal upright T wave in V1** between **7 days** and **6 years** of age signals right ventricular hypertrophy until proven otherwise. Because the neonatal upright T wave should have inverted by the end of the first week, persistence of upright T waves in V1 beyond 7 days reflects abnormal right ventricular strain and should prompt echocardiography.

steps.say: Voltage criteria for chamber enlargement are age dependent, so adult cutoffs mislead in children. Paediatric right ventricular hypertrophy is diagnosed when the R wave in V1 or the S wave in V6 exceeds the 98th percentile for age. In infants, a pure R wave in V1 taller than 10 millimetres makes the diagnosis on its own.
steps.tx: Paediatric **right ventricular hypertrophy criteria** use age indexed voltage percentiles rather than fixed adult cutoffs. The R wave in V1 or the S wave in V6 exceeding the **98th percentile** for age defines RVH, while a pure R wave in V1 above **10 mm** in infants is independently diagnostic and usually reflects severe pressure loading from lesions such as pulmonary stenosis.

vis.alt: QT and voltage panel showing QT lengthening with low calcium and potassium, QT shortening with high calcium, LVH voltage criteria and RVH by R/S ratio over 1 in V1.
vis.caption: Voltage criteria for ventricular hypertrophy with QT interval clues. Diagram from the in-app ECG reference.

steps.say: Left ventricular hypertrophy hides behind different leads from right ventricular hypertrophy. The R wave in V6 or the S wave in V1 must exceed the 98th percentile for the child's age. Deep Q waves over 4 millimetres in V5 and V6, or inverted T waves in V6, add weight and often mark volume loading from a left to right shunt or aortic valve disease.
steps.tx: Paediatric **left ventricular hypertrophy criteria** mirror the right sided rules on the lateral leads. The R wave in V6 or the S wave in V1 above the **98th percentile** for age defines LVH, supported by Q waves deeper than **4 mm** in V5 to V6 or inverted T waves in V6, a pattern commonly produced by large shunts, aortic stenosis, or systemic hypertension.

steps.say: Atrial enlargement leaves its signature on the P wave, and the right atrium declares itself through height. P pulmonale means tall peaked P waves exceeding 2.5 millimetres in lead II at any paediatric age. This finding reflects right atrial overload from tricuspid disease, pulmonary hypertension, or Ebstein anomaly.
steps.tx: **Right atrial enlargement** produces **P pulmonale**, defined as peaked P waves taller than **2.5 mm** in lead II in every paediatric age group. The tall narrow morphology reflects right atrial pressure or volume overload, classically seen with tricuspid stenosis, pulmonary hypertension, and Ebstein anomaly, and it often accompanies right ventricular hypertrophy.

steps.say: While the right atrium grows tall, the overloaded left atrium grows wide and notched. P mitrale is recognised by broad notched P waves that last at least eighty milliseconds in infants and one hundred milliseconds in older children. Lead V1 adds a deep negative terminal deflection as the delayed left atrial vector pulls the second half of the P wave downward.
steps.tx: **Left atrial enlargement** produces **P mitrale** with broad notched P waves of duration **0.08 s** or more in infants and **0.10 s** or more in older children. The P wave in V1 turns biphasic with a deep broad negative terminal deflection, a marker of left atrial volume loading from mitral disease, large left to right shunts, or left ventricular failure.

steps.say: Intervals also mature with age, so a normal PR in a teenager would be long for a baby. The PR interval is eighty to one hundred and twenty milliseconds in infants, and it lengthens to one hundred and twenty to one hundred and sixty milliseconds in adolescents as vagal tone rises and the heart grows. A PR that is short for age hints at preexcitation, while a long one warns of conduction disease or drug effect.
steps.tx: The **normal PR interval evolution** tracks age and resting heart rate throughout childhood. It measures **0.08-0.12 s** in infants and lengthens to **0.12-0.16 s** in adolescents, so adult cutoffs cannot be applied directly. A PR shorter than expected for age suggests an accessory pathway, while prolongation raises concern for first degree block, myocarditis, or digoxin effect.
